How container runtimes actually work

By Jordan Lee · 8 min read

When you run docker run alpine sh, a surprising amount of machinery springs into action. The container image is unpacked, a set of kernel primitives is assembled around the new process, and only then does your shell start.

Namespaces: the illusion of isolation

Namespaces give a process its own view of the system: its own process tree, its own network interfaces, its own mount table. The kernel exposes roughly eight namespace types, and a runtime picks the ones it needs.

The namespace documentation walks through each type in detail. The two most visible are the PID namespace, which makes your container process think it is PID 1, and the network namespace, which hands the container a private stack.

Cgroups: the accounting layer

Control groups bound what a container may consume: CPU shares, memory ceilings, IO budgets. Without them, one noisy container starves its neighbors.

  • CPU bandwidth via cpu.max
  • Memory limits via memory.max
  • Device throughput via the IO controller

The shim layer

High-level runtimes do not talk to the kernel directly. They hand a fully specified bundle to a low-level runtime such as runc, which performs the actual clone and execve dance.

The split matters for operations: the shim keeps the container's stdio flowing even when the daemon restarts. The relevant RFC-style runtime specification spells out the bundle format.

Quick reference

LayerComponentRole
High levelcontainerdImage and lifecycle management
Low levelruncNamespace and cgroup setup
Kernelnamespaces + cgroupsIsolation primitives

Takeaways

A container is not a virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process wrapped in kernel-enforced boundaries, and every tool in the ecosystem is a different convenience layer over those same primitives.

If you want to go deeper, the rest of the series covers networking, storage, and security.
